# Diagnosing Asymmetric Window Motor Behavior on a 2005 Mazda 3

When troubleshooting automotive electrical systems, one of the most frustrating scenarios is when a motor responds perfectly in one direction but remains deadlocked in another. You have swapped components, verified the fuse, and even tested with external power sources, yet the circuit behaves like a broken logic gate: output high for "down," zero voltage for "up." This specific asymmetry on your 2005 Mazda 3 points directly to a control signal issue rather than a power delivery failure.

You have already performed the critical first steps that often stump DIY mechanics. By separating the motor from the regulator and testing it in isolation, you ruled out the mechanical binding or the internal gear train of the regulator. Furthermore, replacing the motor with a Dorman unit confirmed that the actuator itself is not the fault. You also verified the switch by cross-testing with another harness, which isolates the problem to the specific wiring path or the switch's internal logic for the upward motion. The fact that you see 11.84 V on the "down" stroke and a hard drop to zero volts on the "up" stroke is the smoking gun here. In automotive electronics, this isn't a partial failure; it's a complete signal loss on one side of the toggle switch.

Your investigation into the fuse box location for relays (R16-R19) is logical, but it highlights a common misconception about modern automotive architecture. On many platforms, including the Mazda 3 of this era, the window lift motors are not powered directly by the battery through a relay in the passenger cabin. Instead, they utilize a Ground-Operated Switch logic or a dedicated power module located within the door jamb itself. The "relays" you are looking for in the interior fuse box might be non-existent because the control signal comes from the Body Control Module (BCM) or is switched directly via the door switch assembly to ground the motor circuit. If the BCM isn't sending the ground command, or if the internal wiring within the door panel is compromised, the "up" signal will never reach the motor terminals.

The update regarding the driver-side switch provides a definitive answer: the fault lies in the master switch assembly. Window switches are rarely simple SPST (Single Pole Single Throw) toggles; they are multi-position switches that internally route power to different paths based on the direction of the toggle. It is highly probable that one of the internal contacts or the spring-loaded mechanism responsible for the "up" position has corroded or failed, while the "down" circuit remains intact. The fact that physically manipulating the switch restored functionality temporarily confirms that the contact point was simply not making a reliable connection in its resting position.

Replacing all four switches on the driver's door is the correct course of action, as these units are often sold as a matched set to ensure consistent feel and timing across the vehicle. While this involves removing the trim panels and accessing the door jamb connectors, it is a standard repair procedure. Before tearing everything down again, verify the continuity of the wires running from the master switch to the individual door switches. A broken wire in the harness loom can mimic a failed switch, but given your voltage readings, the internal switch failure is the most probable culprit.

For developers working with embedded systems or automotive diagnostics, this scenario serves as a reminder that "zero volts" on an output pin often indicates a missing ground path rather than a missing high signal. Always verify if the load (the motor) is grounded at the chassis or at the control unit before assuming the power source is dead. Once the master switch is replaced and reconnected, you should see the voltage return to the "up" terminal during that specific stroke, restoring full operation to your passenger window.
